title: Sona's strength
hookLine: the mother of ten who ordained late: effort in old age (Therigatha, Sona)

cards: Shame on you, wretched old age. That's how Sona's song ends, and it reads almost like a dare. The path has met her before, in the commentary's story of a late start and a pot of bath water.
Today stays with her own verses. She bore ten sons, she says, and by the time she went to a nun to hear the teaching, she was weak and old. No royal refusal, no dramatic escape.
A tired body, and a decision.

teach.h: TEN SONS, THEN WEAK AND OLD.
teach.b: First, where she started. Having borne ten sons from this body, she says, weak and old, I went to a nun. She doesn't dress it up.
Her strength was gone before her practice began. Second, what she heard. The nun taught her the basics: the heaps that make up a person, the senses, the elements.

teach.h: SHE HEARS, CUTS HER HAIR, GOES.
teach.b: Sona heard it, cut off her hair, and went forth. Nothing in her verses says she waited to feel stronger first. Third, what she found.
While she trained, she says, the divine eye was made clear, and she came to know her former lives.
Her mind became steady and one-pointed. She was freed, clinging to nothing, at peace. The heaps that make up a person, she says, are fully known, and stand now cut off at the root.
Fourth, the dare. Then she turns to old age itself.
Shame on you, she says, wretched old age; there's no more coming back.
Old age had taken her strength of body. It hadn't taken her effort. The strength in the title isn't muscle.
In Sona's song it's the will to keep at it, and it didn't wait for her to be young.

how: In Buddhist communities, people sometimes ordain or take up serious practice late in life, and Sona's verses are remembered as a sign that effort on the path does not depend on youth.

o: a medicine that keeps old age away
the will to keep going, even when old
a body kept strong by years of training

games.q: you're Sona. your children are grown, you're weak and old, and you've just heard a nun teach. what do you do?
o: cut off your hair and go forth.
games.why: she cuts off her hair and goes forth, weak and old as she is, and her song ends with a dare to old age: shame on you, there's no more coming back.

practice: Picture one hard thing sized to the body you have now, a walk you've been putting off, a phone call, a chore that keeps waiting, and see clearly where you'd be and what the first step is.
If a voice says too tired, too old, too late, don't argue with it; just let Sona sit beside it, the nun who started weak and old.

wordCard.voice: Sona's strength. The mother of ten sons who went forth weak and old, was freed, and told old age it had lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali jara: old age. Sona's song ends by telling it: shame on you.

carryVoice: Your line: strength in old age. The body was weak; the effort wasn't. See you tomorrow.
